body: Monday, July 13 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed held rates at its last meeting and leaned toward fighting inflation with future increases rather than cuts. New Chair Kevin Warsh faces his first rate decision at the upcoming July meeting. The curve is positively sloped at +35 bps (10Y at 4.62%, 2Y at 4.21% at the prior close), still flat by historical standards, with both rising over the past four weeks. Fiscal policy remains expansionary while the administration uses equity markets as a scoreboard. VIX at 16.74 signals complacency despite real macro crosscurrents.

New / Most Important: The US-Iran exchange of fire and Trump's reinstatement of the Hormuz blockade escalated the Gulf conflict today, sending oil higher and equities lower. This is a genuine supply-shock catalyst layered on top of a Fed already "genuinely conflicted" on rates. June FOMC minutes released last week showed inflation concerns grew among policymakers. CPI drops tomorrow (July 14) — the signal feed flags it as a "big deal for the stock market." Retail investors have been cashing out of Apple, Tesla, and chip stocks, a notable positioning shift. Meanwhile, public companies have been issuing new shares at an elevated pace, absorbing liquidity even as the index grinds higher.

Playbook ✓: S&P 500 at 7528 continues its grind higher (+1.8% over 4W) despite macro headwinds — the classic "bad news is tolerated until it isn't" pattern. Rising yields and rising equities coexist as long as earnings deliver.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The Hormuz blockade reinstatement is structurally new and potentially market-regime-changing. This is not a standard Gulf tension flare-up — a US-imposed blockade on the Strait of Hormuz directly constrains roughly 20% of global oil transit, creating an administered supply shock rather than a market-driven one. Oil has already dropped 13.6% over four weeks (likely pre-blockade oversupply dynamics from OPEC's +3.05M bpd June production surge), but the blockade narrative now clashes violently with that bearish positioning. The growth pulse backs the supply-shock reading: US ISM manufacturing was still expanding at 53.3 in June and China's official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.3, so this is not a demand collapse. If sustained, this forces the Fed into a stagflationary corner: rising energy costs suppress growth while preventing rate cuts. The rate-sensitive end of the growth pulse is already softening — US existing home sales unexpectedly fell in June as the 30-year mortgage rate rose to 6.49% — so markets are right to price defensive hedges over cyclical optimism. Watch for a rapid repricing of rate-cut expectations into rate-hike expectations if CPI tomorrow prints hot on energy pass-through.
Macro Stance: The ECB appears to be in pause mode after recent Eurozone data supported holding steady. The economy remains weak but monetary easing expectations have been dialed back.

New / Most Important: The Economist flagged European markets as "a steal" despite the economic mess — a contrarian capital-flow setup. EUR/USD edged lower on divergent central bank signals, consistent with an ECB pause while other central banks stay hawkish. An international ETF (likely Europe-heavy) is reportedly beating the S&P 500 in 2026.

Playbook ✓: Cheap European equities attracting value flows while the macro backdrop remains sluggish — textbook relative-value rotation.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The Hormuz escalation is an acute negative for Europe given its energy import dependency. If the US is actively blockading the strait, European energy costs spike disproportionately, potentially forcing the ECB to pause longer than the economy can tolerate.

Macro Stance: The PBOC pledged to keep policy accommodative amid weak demand and external shocks (Reuters, [Jul 8]) while flagging "structural divergences" as the AI boom masks consumer weakness (BigGo Finance, [Jul 9]). The currency is moving the other way: the PBOC set its strongest fix in three years (Business Recorder, [Jul 9]), then took the fixing below 6.8 per dollar for the first time since 2023 (Bloomberg, [Jul 10]). Prices are split: June CPI rose 1% (Global Times, [Jul 9]) and slowed more than forecast (Bloomberg, [Jul 8]), while producer inflation jumped to a four-year high (Reuters, [Jul 8]). The lean is bullish on policy and flows, not on household demand.

PMIs & Activity: The June official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.3 (Reuters, [Jun 29]) and non-manufacturing to 50.2 (Reuters, [Jun 29]); the private survey capped the strongest factory quarter since late 2020 (Reuters, [Jun 30]), while services activity slowed slightly (Reuters, [Jul 2]). May's hard data show the split underneath: industrial output growth quickened but retail sales and investment contracted (Reuters, [Jun 15]), with retail sales down 0.6%, the first decline since 2022 (Il Sole 24 Ore, [Jun 15]). Going into this week's releases, a Reuters poll expects June export growth to cool, with AI demand underpinning strength ([Jul 12]), and surveys see second-quarter growth slowing (Daily Sabah, [Jul 12]). The IMF nonetheless lifted its 2026 forecast to 4.6% (Global Times, [Jul 8]).

Credit Impulse: May total social financing grew 7.7% (CGTN, [Jun 12]) and topped forecasts (Bloomberg, [Jun 12]), but new loans missed as the property slump curbed demand (Reuters, [Jun 12]) and households kept deleveraging (SCMP, [Jun 15]). The impulse is government bonds, not private borrowing. Regulators are now leaning against the riskier end of the bond market: a crackdown on inflated AAA ratings (Caixin, [Jul 7]) leaves up to 494.6 billion yuan of bonds facing downgrade risk (BigGo Finance, [Jul 8]), and bankers were asked to avoid underwriting short-term LGFV bonds (Bloomberg, [Jul 8]). With June data due this week (WSJ, [Jul 10]), the read going in is a flat headline impulse and a negative private one.

Property: New home prices fell at a faster pace in May (Reuters, [Jun 15]) even as first-tier prices rose for a third month (SCMP, [Jun 16]), and real-estate investment fell 16.2% y/y in January–May (GMK Center, [Jun 18]). June brought no turn: a private survey shows resale prices falling faster (Reuters, [Jun 30]), while top-100 developer sales up 11.8% month-on-month in June (Moomoo, [Jul 1]) look seasonal. Developer stress is back: Vanke says its first-half loss may widen to $2.2 billion (Bloomberg, [Jul 10]), and Fitch sees new home sales falling 11% to 13% this year (Mingtiandi, [Jul 9]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Beijing finalised its 2026 list of key national projects (China Daily, [Jul 7]) and Bloomberg sees a chance at a fiscal rethink after the debt-cleanup milestone ([Jul 9]), but Societe Generale describes the support as targeted (FXStreet, [Jul 10]). On trade, the thaw with Washington continues, with China dropping a 10% tariff on US farm goods including soybeans (AgWeb, [Jul 6]). Friction with Brussels is rising instead: EU duties of up to 45 per cent on Chinese tyres (Eunews, [Jul 9]), an anti-dumping probe into ducks (SCMP, [Jul 10]) and contingency measures for a trade war (The Brussels Times, [Jul 11]). A temporary helium export ban (SCMP, [Jul 10]) shows export controls remain Beijing's lever.

Markets & Flows: Hong Kong is set for its strongest week in over a year on China internet gains (The Business Times, [Jul 10]), after Chinese stocks in HK jumped the most in 14 months (Bloomberg, [Jul 7]); SCMP's report of overseas capital pouring into hard-tech giants fits the same pattern. The mainland lags: stocks hit a four-week low (TradingView, [Jul 8]) and fell as the week began (TradingView, [Jul 12]), and China's biggest ETF is now a US$13 billion gold fund as state stock-market support fades (The Business Times, [Jul 6]).

New / Most Important: The yuan is the signal going into a heavy data week. A fixing below 6.8 for the first time since 2023, from a central bank that promises accommodation, means Beijing is accepting currency strength just as the Reuters poll expects export growth to cool and surveys see the second quarter slowing. A firmer yuan imports disinflation into a CPI already at 1% and squeezes the southern factories that SCMP says are feeling the pinch despite a pickup in orders ([Jul 12]). The bullish case rests on flows into Hong Kong tech and hard-tech names, not on a domestic turn, which is why this week's trade, credit and GDP prints matter more than usual.

Playbook ✓: An accommodative PBOC, targeted rather than broad stimulus, a property drag and an export-led PMI are all on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The consensus reads a strong yuan and a Hong Kong rally as reflation; the growth pulse says China is still exporting its excess supply. The June PMI is export-led, private credit is contracting and property investment is falling by double digits, so domestic absorption is not improving. Yuan strength is supporting AUD (Mitrade, [Jul 10]) and global iron ore trade hit a record on Chinese demand (S&P Global, [Jul 10]), but with new home sales seen falling 11% to 13%, construction-led steel demand is fading and that support looks cyclical. European exporters face the sharper edge, as tyre duties and duck probes are the visible part of a trade gap that a firmer yuan narrows only at the margin, while EM Asia rides the AI export cycle. A real turn needs loan growth, not bond issuance, to re-accelerate; until it does, Hong Kong's rally is flows, not fundamentals.

Macro Stance: The BOJ is firmly on a tightening path. Producer prices hit the fastest pace since 2023, wholesale inflation at three-year highs, and the BOJ is expected to raise its growth forecast while maintaining vigilance on inflation.

New / Most Important: Japan spent $73.7 billion to support the yen and it is "barely working" — this is the critical development. USDJPY is eyeing 175. Multiple outlets are now calling this a "slow motion currency crisis." Japan signaled a massive pension shift to domestic assets, sparking a rally in yen and bonds — this is GPIF-scale capital repatriation, a structural flow event. The Nikkei dropped 2.14% today amid cautious sentiment.

Playbook ✓: BOJ hikes → yen should strengthen → carry trade unwinds. The pension repatriation signal fits this narrative.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The pension repatriation signal is the most structurally important development in this feed. Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund shifting allocation toward domestic assets represents potentially hundreds of billions of dollars in cross-border flow reversal. For decades, GPIF and Japan Post were the marginal buyer of foreign bonds — particularly US Treasuries and European govvies. If Japan is now pulling that capital home, it removes a critical source of demand for global fixed income at exactly the moment US yields are already climbing (10Y at 4.62%, up 16 bps in 4 weeks). This is a structural tightening of global dollar liquidity that has nothing to do with the Fed. The yen intervention's failure despite $73.7B spent suggests the BOJ needs much higher rates to stabilize the currency, which means more domestic asset demand and more foreign asset liquidation. This is the single biggest capital-flow story in global macro right now.

Macro Stance: The RBA is actively hawkish. Chief economist warned of more frequent supply shocks. Board member Hunter stated the RBA "will intervene as necessary" to bring inflation back to target. Westpac now sees one more RBA hike before any cuts.

New / Most Important: The RBA's explicit supply-shock framing is new and important — it provides intellectual cover for tightening even if demand weakens. AUD/USD edged higher to near 0.6950 on hawkish rhetoric. House prices and bank stocks are flagged as vulnerable.

Playbook ✓: Hawkish RBA + strong AUD is textbook.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Westpac calling for another hike is a domestic consensus break — most had expected the next move to be a cut. If the RBA hikes into a housing market already showing stress, this becomes a policy accident risk. The supply-shock framework the RBA is adopting effectively says "we will tighten regardless of demand conditions," which in a highly leveraged household sector is playing with fire.

Macro Stance: Rates stay at 3.75% after last week's hold (PAP Biznes, [Jul 8]), and the market is still digesting Governor Glapiński's offer to file a cut motion after the summer (StockWatch.pl, [Jul 9]) against a projection that lifts 2027 inflation and lowers growth (Analizy.pl, [Jul 10]). Monday's data added a softer growth note: GUS industrial figures show Polish industry "standing still", with declines outnumbering gains across branches even as a few sectors post records (Forsal.pl, wnp.pl, Business Insider Polska, [Jul 13]). On prices, shelf inflation decelerated for another month in a row (Agro Profil, [Jul 13]), consistent with inflation sitting inside the NBP target (XYZ, [Jul 9]), while the NBP's own report warns of a new supply shock working through to shops (Wiadomości Handlowe, [Jul 11]). The Council's split is the constraint: two members told Reuters there is no rush to cut after summer ([Jul 10]) and Erste sees no move before end-2027 (Direct Money, [Jul 10]). PKO BP still expects 3.5% GDP growth this year (wnp.pl, [Jul 11]). Transmission is already loosening without a cut: banks are "massively" cutting mortgage rates and offers starting with a five are back (Bankier.pl, [Jul 13]).

Markets: Monday extended the record run but with a different engine. Orlen, lifted by rising oil, pulled WIG20 to new highs "in a difficult environment" and energy names drove the session (Bankier.pl, Inwestycje.pl, XYZ, [Jul 13]), while copper fell on the Hormuz conflict and KGHM came under pressure again (Business Insider Polska, [Jul 13]). Friday's card had PKO 112.88 (+7.3% 1W, +7.9% 4W) and Pekao 244.3 (+4.8% / +7.1%) after Goldman's upgrade (pb.pl, [Jul 10]), Orlen 139.92 (+5.3% / -4.7%), KGHM 308.95 (-7.8% / -14.4%), PGE 9.37 (-2.6% / -6.2%), Allegro 39.83 (+3.6% / +15.7%), Dino 28.22, CD Projekt 233.0, LPP 19380, and EPOL 40.37 (+2.4% / +3.8%). The zloty had a worse morning than the index: the dollar is the most expensive in 14 months and the zloty is "under pressure from the war over the Strait of Hormuz" (Bankier.pl, [Jul 13]), with USD/PLN at 3.7944 (+1.2% 1W, +3.8% 4W) and EUR/PLN 4.3271 (+0.9% / +2.0%) on the card. Business Insider reports the zloty broke its losing streak, with economists attaching one condition ([Jul 13]), and ING's EMEA FX note argues zloty weakness "looks temporary" ([Jul 13]); CEO Magazyn warns it may be a difficult week as the dollar waits for a US impulse ([Jul 13]). POLGB yields had eased on the dovish signals per PKO BP (wnp.pl, [Jul 10]).

Fiscal & Politics: Brussels opened an excessive-deficit procedure against Bulgaria over a record deficit (Business Insider Polska, Money.pl, [Jul 13]), a warning shot for a Polish finance minister who already calls the deficit the main obstacle to tax cuts before an election-year budget (Money.pl, [Jul 9]). The PIT threshold fight continues, with pb.pl expecting only modest gains for scale taxpayers ([Jul 13]). Germany plans a large rise in army spending, pulling well ahead of Poland (Business Insider Polska, [Jul 13]). A coalition quarrel surfaced around Petru (wPolityce.pl, [Jul 13]). On the plus side, Warsaw will host a new ESA security centre and BGK is launching a space investment fund (SpaceNews, Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK, [Jul 13]).

Corporate & Sectors: Allegro grew second-quarter EBITDA by 11.5% with record growth abroad (XYZ, pb.pl, [Jul 13]). Orlen's Grudziądz CCGT started feeding the grid, days after Baltic Power's first offshore power (WysokieNapiecie.pl, [Jul 13]; PAP Biznes, [Jul 10]); the company appointed Diana Batko to the board (Bankier.pl, [Jul 13]) and Bogdanka extended its coal contract with Orlen Termika to 2028 (StockWatch.pl, [Jul 13]). KGHM secured a 64 million zloty NFOŚiGW loan for 19.4 MW of solar (Strefa Inwestorów, [Jul 13]) after a weekend of mine tremors that ended with all miners safe (Portal Samorządowy, [Jul 11]) and a 32 billion zloty investment plan to 2030 (pb.pl, [Jul 9]). The energy ministry talks of 1 trillion zloty for the transition and sees scope for lower power prices in 2027 (wnp.pl, XYZ, [Jul 13]), Tauron detailed a 7 billion zloty project and signed on Rożnów II (Portal Samorządowy, TVP Kraków, [Jul 13]), and negative power prices are setting records (WysokieNapiecie.pl, [Jul 13]). Dino shares fell amid a dispute with employees and the GIS poppy-seed recall (wPolityce.pl, Gov.pl, [Jul 13]). Banks: PKO BP is launching settlements on euro-denominated loans (Franknews.pl, [Jul 13]) on top of 297 million zloty of Q2 CHF provisions (Bankier.pl, [Jul 10]).

Geopolitics & Security: Sikorski told Poles there is "no panic": Russia lacks the capacity to attack Poland but is preparing something (Kyiv Post, Ukrainska Pravda, [Jul 13]), as France summoned Russia's ambassador over sabotage in a dozen European countries (CBS News, [Jul 13]). US Army troop rotations to Poland are back on, for now (The National Interest, [Jul 9]). The Ukraine file is deteriorating at home: a Rzeczpospolita poll finds more Poles against than for sending weapons ([Jul 12]), and Poland says Ukraine could start producing missiles within weeks (The New Voice of Ukraine, [Jul 9]).

New / Most Important: The oil-driven leadership rotation is the day's signal. A record index led by Orlen on Hormuz-linked crude, while copper and the zloty fall on the same conflict, means Warsaw is now trading as an energy-shock market rather than a rate-cut market. That is less comfortable than last week's bank-led rally: the dovish pivot plus an oil shock is precisely the combination the July projection flagged as lifting 2027 inflation, and it makes the "temporary" zloty weakness thesis dependent on the Gulf rather than the NBP.

Playbook ✓: Dovish shift plus stronger dollar equals weaker zloty, as expected; Orlen bid on higher crude is standard.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Cutting rates while projecting higher inflation is a credibility risk, and an oil shock imported through a weaker zloty would compound it, creating the self-reinforcing loop of currency weakness and inflation that the Council's hawks fear. Industry stalling while the index sets records is a second gap that earnings season will have to close.

Macro Stance: KOSPI tumbled below 7,000 in a "Black Monday" sell-off today — Korean equities are taking the brunt of the chip selloff and Gulf escalation. Vietnam is at a capital market "turning point" with structural reform momentum.

New / Most Important: Korea's sell-off reflects the double hit of semiconductor weakness and energy import cost fears from the Hormuz situation. Vietnam's market development story continues to attract frontier-to-EM upgrade flows.
Playbook ✓: Korea as high-beta to global chip/trade cycle, performing accordingly.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: None today.
Narrative: The AI trade is under capex scrutiny: the Nasdaq 100 is down 0.3% over 4 weeks, lagging the S&P and Russell, and the story has shifted from revenue excitement to margin-compression fears.

Reported: TCS topped revenue estimates on a weak rupee and a banking boost (Reuters, [Jul 9]), and the shares jumped 4% as analysts bet on deal wins (Business Standard, [Jul 10]). Foxconn Industrial Internet forecast first-half net profit up by as much as 100%, with AI server revenue rising over 230% (Moomoo, [Jul 9]). Endava cut guidance after a Q3 miss (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 9]).

EPS Upside Watch: Apple — JPMorgan raised its target as robust demand protects revenue from recent hardware price hikes (TIKR.com, [Jul 8]): pricing power into the print. Data-infrastructure software — Citi's Q2 preview sees AI budgets concentrating on these leaders (Moomoo, [Jul 12]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Retail, long the marginal buyer of mega-cap tech, is cashing out of Apple and Tesla; institutional flows alone may not sustain multiples, and a Russell/Nasdaq ratio up 1.5% over 4W says the rotation is real.
Narrative: Meta's rising AI capex is the sector's key headwind and Netflix "continues to disappoint", so the mega-cap platforms trade on spending discipline rather than on growth.
Reported: No major reports this week. Netflix, down 42% from its high, reports on July 16 (The Motley Fool, [Jul 7]).
EPS Upside Watch: Alibaba — the shares jumped the most in ten months as earnings hopes grow (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 8]), with half-year reports set to test AI monetisation (BigGo Finance, [Jul 8]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: In Hong Kong, capital is rotating out of AI hardware into internet stocks (BigGo Finance, [Jul 7]) — the reverse of the US, where platforms are punished for capex. If that holds, the cheaper Chinese platforms, not the US mega-caps, get paid first for AI monetisation.

Narrative: A 10Y at 4.62% and a 2Y at 4.21% leave a positively sloped but still-flat +35 bps curve, a modest NIM tailwind, while the SpaceX IPO and elevated equity issuance keep the capital-markets revenue cycle active.

Reported: The big US banks have not reported yet; JPMorgan kicks off on July 14 (The Motley Fool, [Jul 10]). In India, Indian Bank's Q1 net profit rose 10% (Business Standard, [Jul 10]) and the shares jumped 10% (BusinessLine, [Jul 10]), while HDFC Bank led the market after strong Q1 growth (Reuters, [Jul 6]).

EPS Upside Watch: Wall Street trading desks — a trading surge, helped by the SpaceX IPO, is seen lifting the big banks' second-quarter earnings (Reuters, [Jul 7]). European investment banks — IB fees had their strongest first half since 2021 (TheBanker.com, [Jul 7]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Australian banks are flagged as vulnerable to house-price declines as the RBA leans toward another hike. In leveraged housing markets the higher-rates tailwind can turn into a credit-loss headwind quickly.

Narrative: Refiners rallied on the reinstated Hormuz blockade. WTI at $75.80 is still down 13.6% over 4 weeks on OPEC oversupply, but the blockade adds an acute supply-disruption premium that favours refiners running non-Gulf crude.

Reported: Exxon signalled a Q2 profit windfall as higher oil prices boost the bottom line (Reuters, [Jul 7]). Shell raised Q2 gas output guidance and flagged stronger gas trading results (Reuters, [Jul 7]), and the shares gained (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 7]).

EPS Upside Watch: Devon Energy — earnings expectations have been upgraded on estimate revisions (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 10]). Valero and Marathon Petroleum — a blockade-driven widening of crack spreads raises product prices faster than input costs.

⚡ Breaking Convention: A June OPEC output jump of 3.05M bpd is colliding with a blockade of roughly 20% of global oil transit, so Gulf barrels cannot reach market: the Brent-WTI spread should widen and Atlantic-basin crude decouple. With US ISM at 53.3 and China's official PMI at 50.3, demand is not the swing variable — supply is.

Narrative: Small caps lead (Russell +1.1% vs Nasdaq -0.3%), giving domestic industrials a breadth bid, while rising energy costs from the Gulf escalation are the margin headwind; defence is the implicit Hormuz beneficiary.

Reported: Delta beat Q2 estimates as travel demand withstood higher prices (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 10]) and reinstated full-year guidance, but the shares slid as fuel prices bite (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 10]). DHL beat Q2 expectations and raised full-year guidance (DHL Group, [Jul 7]) on an express recovery (WWD, [Jul 9]). Honeywell raised its profit guidance (Reuters, [Jul 9]).

EPS Upside Watch: Truckers — analysts are raising truckload and LTL estimates ahead of Q2 (FreightWaves, [Jul 10]). United Airlines — expected to beat estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 8]) with ticket prices up 15-20% (24/7 Wall St., [Jul 10]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Airlines are meant to be fuel victims, yet Delta says higher airfares will last even as oil prices fall (The Guardian, [Jul 10]). If that pricing power holds, fares, not jet fuel, set the group's margins this season.

Narrative: Consumer stress is migrating from discretionary to staples as more Americans struggle to repay card bills for groceries, and rising energy costs from the Hormuz escalation will squeeze discretionary budgets further.

Reported: Levi Strauss beat, raised guidance and lifted its dividend (CNBC, [Jul 8]) as its DTC shift pays off (WSJ, [Jul 8]). Fast Retailing's Q3 profit jumped 45.7% and it raised its forecast (The Straits Times, [Jul 9]), though the shares slid on a yen warning (NST Online, [Jul 9]). Trent tumbled 12% as Q1 revenue missed (Rediff MoneyWiz, [Jul 7]).

EPS Upside Watch: Tesla — UBS raised its target and expects a strong Q2 beat (TipRanks, [Jul 11]) after the best monthly deliveries of 2026 (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 8]). Aritzia — raised its 2027 guidance after beating on adjusted profit (BNN Bloomberg, [Jul 10]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: Retail investors are selling Tesla, a top XLY holding, so retail liquidation is a sector-level headwind even as the sell side sets up for a beat.
Narrative: Defensive rotation should help staples as geopolitical risk rises, but grocery cost inflation, visible in the card-repayment stress, is a margin headwind for food retailers and brands.

Reported: PepsiCo's Q2 sales beat estimates (TradingView, [Jul 9]), but it warned of higher commodity costs amid faltering North American food sales (Reuters, [Jul 9]). WD-40 beat Q3 forecasts and the shares jumped after hours (Investing.com, [Jul 9]). Simply Good Foods topped earnings and revenue estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 9]).
EPS Upside Watch: Seven & i — the 7-Eleven owner raised guidance as gas earnings rose at its North America unit (WSJ, [Jul 9]), a fuel-margin tailwind.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Staples are the supposed shelter from an energy shock, yet PepsiCo says shoppers are 'worse than anticipated' on gas prices (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 9]). Volume elasticity, not just input costs, is now the sector's risk.
Narrative: With no sector-specific catalyst, defensive positioning should support healthcare in a risk-off tape as geopolitical tension rises, while a 10Y at 4.62% caps multiples.
Reported: No major reports this week.

EPS Upside Watch: Johnson & Johnson — the shares gained on a higher outlook and pre-earnings optimism (Quiver Quantitative, [Jul 7]), with its MedTech segment eyeing another strong quarter (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 6]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Eli Lilly's $400 billion surge is reshaping Big Pharma (24/7 Wall St., [Jul 9]): the "defensive" label now hides a concentrated growth trade, so the sector's earnings path depends on a few names more than on rates.

Narrative: Copper at $6.28 is flat over 4 weeks (+0.3%) and trades as an AI data-centre and grid-capex metal. For construction materials the read comes from PMIs and property: China's official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.3 in June, but real-estate investment fell 16.2% y/y in January–May and Fitch sees new home sales falling 11% to 13% this year.

Reported: Covestro raised its 2026 core earnings outlook after a strong first half (Reuters, [Jul 9]). Zijin Mining's first-half profit surged 170% (finance.biggo.com, [Jul 9]). Fletcher Building lifted its fiscal 2026 EBIT guidance (Yahoo Finance Australia, [Jul 8]).

EPS Upside Watch: Neo Performance Materials — the rare-earth processor raised full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance (PR Newswire Canada, [Jul 8]), as China stalls Japan-bound exports of critical minerals (Japan Wire by Kyodo News, [Jul 6]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The upgrades are coming from chemicals, the sector's laggard: Covestro lifted its outlook and Morningstar sees opportunities in chemicals (Morningstar, [Jul 9]), while construction-linked names wait for China's 2026 key national projects to turn into spending.

Narrative: Rising 10Y yields (4.62%, up 16 bps over 4W) are a direct headwind to rate-sensitive REITs, and housing is softening: US existing home sales unexpectedly fell in June as the 30-year mortgage rate rose to 6.49%.

Reported: UK homebuilder Vistry's shares plunged on a warning of first-half losses (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 8]) as its CFO exits (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 8]). China Vanke says its first-half loss may widen to $2.2 billion (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 10]).
EPS Upside Watch: Schroder REIT — portfolio vacancies are at a four-year low as the Picton acquisition continues (Investment Week, [Jul 10]), supporting rental income.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Bids are rising, not falling: LondonMetric and Schroder REIT raised their offer for Picton (Property Week, [Jul 10]) and Glenstone lifted its bid for Alternative Income REIT (QuotedData, [Jul 6]). Buyers see value where the rate-driven consensus sees only duration risk.

Narrative: Rising yields make utility dividends less attractive on a relative basis; the AI power-demand story is a secular tailwind, but for now it is fighting a 10Y at 4.62%, up 16 bps over 4W, as the Fed leans hawkish.
Reported: No major reports this week.
EPS Upside Watch: Vistra — long-term PPAs are seen as a growth catalyst (TradingView, [Jul 9]), locking in contracted power sales.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Data-centre demand has investors re-evaluating US electric utility stocks (S&P Global, [Jul 10]). If the group is re-rated as a growth sector rather than a bond proxy, the rate headwind matters less than the consensus assumes.

Mechanically, both episodes feature a beaten-down commodity (oil was depressed pre-catalyst), a sudden geopolitical shock creating a supply-constraint narrative, and retail rotating out of growth/tech into the "obvious" beneficiary. The 2022 analog also shows the risk: oil peaked within months as demand destruction and SPR releases crushed the thesis, and latecomers were badly burned.

Professional energy traders know that Hormuz threats have historically been resolved short of full closure, making the tail risk priced by retail far more extreme than probability-weighted models suggest.
